newsitem.title: TOGO: Zaire talks in next days but no prior ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks in next days but no prior ceasefire.

text.p: Zaire's rebels announced imminent negotiations with President Mobutu Sese Seko's shaky regime on Thursday but resisted pressure to accept a prior ceasefire.
A two-day African summit on the Zaire crisis ended with a statement calling for immediate negotiations between the warring parties but did not insist on a ceasefire before the talks.

"We are very excited to learn that for the first time the people from Kinshasa (Zaire's capital) have decided to agree on a starting of the negotiations which are going to be in a very few days to come," Bizima Karaha, the senior rebel delegate at the summit in Togo, told a news conference.
Five months into their revolt, Laurent Kabila's disciplined fighters control about a quarter of Zaire.
With copper-rich Shaba province now in their sights, the rebels have refused international pressure to agree a ceasefire before negotiations with Mobutu's camp.
They stuck to the position in Lome and appeared to have won the argument.

In a final declaration, the African presidents "called for immediate negotiations between the government of Zaire and the Democratic Alliance for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), leading to a ceasefire and complete cessation of hostilites".
South Africa or Togo were the likely venues for the talks.
Delegates from the warring factions met separately with the presidents of Nigeria, Togo and Cameroon and U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan, diplomatic sources said.
Mobutu, who returned home last Friday after fresh cancer treatment in Europe, has seen his grip on the country he has dominated since a 1965 coup weaken.
But Karaha said he remained a player. "There are some people who have a little power (left), in particular Mobutu and we would like to negotiate with him," he added.
"It's in his interests to negotiate his own departure," Gaetan Kakudji, the other Kabila representative in Lome, said.

There was no firm idea of the agenda of the imminent talks or indeed the participants. Mobutu is president but the opposition parties in Kinshasa also expect to be involved in negotiations with Kabila's rebel alliance.
In rebel-held Kisangani, the popular mood was for Kabila's men to press on with their advance.

Senior rebel sources there told Reuters there can be no ceasefire before negotiations in the form of a summit between Mobutu and Kabila, but they are willing to start talks between rival delegations to prepare the summit.
Privately, senior alliance officials dismissed the Lome summit and said they favoured a South African peace initiative.
The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit gave the rebels their first major international platform.
Kabila scored more points in Paris when France changed its tone, dropping the term "rebels" and referring to them for the first time by their chosen name.
The subtle shift by Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt followed Wednesday night's meeting between the Mobutu and Kabila delegates in Lome.
France has remained loyal to Mobutu throughout the rebellion but appears to have accepted there is now a high risk his 32-year reign is ending.
Host Togo hailed the meeting between the rival delegates, in Annan's presence, as an historic breakthrough.
But Kakudji said it was symbolic only. "Apart from a handshake in front of the (Togolese) president we haven't exchanged the slightest word."
France and the United States, which with Belgium have sent troops to the region to evacuate their nationals if violence erupts in Kinshasa, lobbied jointly in Lome for a truce and talks.

Diplomatic pressure focused on a five point peace plan formulated by U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun. The summit's final declaration said the talks and subsequent ceasefire should pave the way for implementation of the Sahnoun plan, which Kinshasa has already accepted.
One of the plan's points is for urgent action to help up to 370,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees of the Hutu tribe stranded in eastern Zaire by the fighting.
The U.N. refugee agency reported alarming death rates among refugees at two sites and said the toll would only worsen unless rebels allow aid agencies to bring in more aid.

"The mortality rate at Tingi Tingi is 153 per 10,000 per day and at Amisi 48 per 10,000 per day. Refugees in a camp should be at between five and 10 deaths per 10,000 per day," UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said in rebel-held Kisangani.
"A mortality rate of 153 is very alarming. It is imperative the (rebel) alliance let us in to establish proper feeding to give these people care before they are repatriated," he said.
